about.title: Spreading across the world
about.length_note: About 25 minutes. The class follows four routes (Asia, Australia, Europe, the Americas), and the Americas are the most argued, so they get the most beats. Each site gets its own short beat. If you are short on time, skip the Apidima beats (4 and 5) and the Monte Verde beats (27 and 28). Everything else builds on the beats before it.

say.text: Last class we met our species and its cousins. Today we follow Homo sapiens as it spreads into Asia, Australia, Europe and the Americas.

show.text: Spreading across the world

say.text: We will also see why the dates are argued over. That part matters as much as the routes.

show.text: Migration: a group of people moving to live somewhere new

say.text: First, a key idea. 'Earliest known' means the oldest site found so far. It does not mean the first person who ever arrived.

show.text: Earliest known = oldest site found so far

say.text: New finds can move a date back. One dig in northern Australia pushed the date of arrival back by up to 18,000 years.

show.text: Up to 18,000 years pushed back

ask.right: The oldest site that has been found so far
wrong: The exact day the first person arrived
The oldest site that could ever exist
The site with the most tools
ask.why: A new dig can always find something older, so 'earliest known' can change.

say.text: Homo sapiens began in Africa. A few early groups left long before the main exit. A jaw from Misliya Cave in Israel is 177,000 to 194,000 years old.

show.text: An upper jaw with teeth, found in Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, Israel

say.text: Apidima Cave in Greece is a site in its own right. Two skulls were found there in the late 1970s but stayed puzzling for decades.

show.text: Two incomplete, distorted fossil skulls from Apidima Cave, southern Greece

say.text: In 2019, new analysis said one skull, about 210,000 years old, was an early Homo sapiens. The other was a Neanderthal, about 40,000 years younger. The researchers think this early group died out, and Neanderthals later lived there instead.

show.text: Apidima, the site twice | Skulls made their owners' lives about 210,000 years ago | Found late 1970s, understood in 2019

ask.q: Why do the researchers think this early group did not found today's non-African populations?
ask.right: They think it died out and was probably replaced by Neanderthals
wrong: It sailed to Australia
It was never found
It turned into Neanderthals
ask.why: The skull is much older than the main exit, and a younger Neanderthal skull is in the same cave. Researchers read that as a failed early move out of Africa.

say.text: The exit that matters for most people alive outside Africa came later. Genetic studies point to a move beginning some 50,000 to 60,000 years ago.

show.text: 50,000 to 60,000 years ago

say.text: Other summaries say 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. So scientists do not give one number, and we say a range.

show.text: 70,000 to 50,000 years ago

ask.q: Roughly when did the main exit from Africa happen?
wrong: About 5,000 years ago
About 500,000 years ago
About 20,000 years ago
ask.why: Different studies give slightly different dates, but they overlap in the range of about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago.

say.text: One common model has people following the southern coast of Asia. They reached Oceania by about 50,000 years ago.

show.text: An arrow from East Africa along the southern coast of Asia, then south-east to Oceania

say.text: Here is our class on one line. Early exits, the main exit, Australia, Europe, then the Americas.

show.text: About 200,000 years ago: early exits | 70,000 to 50,000: main exit | 50,000 or more: Australia | About 45,000: Europe | 23,000 to 14,500: the Americas (argued)

say.text: Let us go to Australia first. Sahul is the old continent that existed when sea levels were low: Australia, New Guinea and the Aru Islands, joined.

show.text: Sahul: Australia + New Guinea + Aru Islands, joined at low sea level

say.text: Reaching Sahul still took several sea crossings through the islands of Wallacea. At least one crossing was close to 100 kilometres.

show.text: Sunda (south-east Asia) on the left, a chain of Wallacean islands, then Sahul on the right, with sea gaps between

ask.right: It needed several crossings of open sea
wrong: It was joined to Asia by a land bridge
It was reached through the ice-free corridor
It needed no boats at all
ask.why: The Wallacean islands were not joined by land, so people had to cross water, at least once about 100 kilometres.

say.text: Did they drift there by accident? A 2019 model says random drifting almost never works. The chance is under 5% unless 40 or more adults were washed off an island every 20 years.

show.text: Under 5% by chance

say.text: Choosing when to leave and steering a little raised the odds a lot. The authors conclude people could plan open-sea voyages by 50,000 years ago. Whether these particular crossings were planned is unknown.

show.text: Pick a time to leave | Paddle a little toward the target | Odds of arriving go up

ask.q: What raised the chance of arriving, in the model?
ask.right: Choosing when to leave and making a little headway toward land
wrong: Waiting for a land bridge to appear
Travelling only in large ships with sails
Following the coast of Europe
ask.why: The model found that picking a departure time and steering a little greatly increased the chance of arriving.

say.text: Now a site. Madjedbebe is a rock shelter in Mirarr Country, about 300 kilometres east of Darwin, at the foot of the Arnhem Land escarpment.

show.text: A sandstone rock shelter at the base of a rocky escarpment on a sandy plain, Northern Territory, Australia

say.text: Here is Madjedbebe twice. A 2017 study says people lived there about 65,000 years ago, using grinding stones, ground ochre and ground-edge axe heads.

show.text: Madjedbebe, the site twice | Lived in: about 65,000 years ago (disputed) | Dug: 1970s, again in 1989, and again for the 2017 study

say.text: How do you date sand? The team dated the sand grains themselves and checked against radiocarbon where they could. Charcoal there runs out at about 45,000 years.

show.text: Dated the sand grains | Checked against radiocarbon where possible | Charcoal runs out at about 45,000 years

ask.q: Why could radiocarbon not date the oldest layers at Madjedbebe?
ask.right: The charcoal runs out at about 45,000 years, so older layers needed another method
wrong: Radiocarbon only works on stone
Nobody in Australia owned the equipment
The sand was too wet
ask.why: Radiocarbon on charcoal only reached about 45,000 years at the site, so the older dates came from the sand grains.

say.text: Not everyone accepts 65,000. Archaeologists Jim Allen and James O'Connell say the sand was disturbed, so younger tools could have sunk into older sand.

show.text: Disputed | For: dates the sand at 65,000 | Against: the sand was disturbed, so it looks too old

say.text: Their 2025 paper says the other oldest Sahul sites cluster between about 43,000 and 54,000 years ago. The dig team says disturbance was small and termites did not rework the deposit.

show.text: Allen and O'Connell: no reliable support before about 50,000 | Dig team: only small disturbance

ask.q: What is the Madjedbebe argument mainly about?
ask.right: Whether disturbed sand makes the tools look older than they are
wrong: Whether Australia was ever settled
Whether Madjedbebe is in Australia
Whether anyone used stone tools
ask.why: Both sides accept people lived there. They disagree on whether the sand was shuffled and the old date is too old.

say.text: Here are the two dates side by side. Careful scientists stand behind each one.

show.text: Two views on when people reached Australia

say.text: Now Europe. Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria holds some of the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens in Europe.

show.text: The mouth of Bacho Kiro Cave in the foothills of the Balkan Mountains, Bulgaria

say.text: Fossils reported in 2020 are directly dated to about 45,000 years ago. They lay with stone tools, bone tools, hunted animal remains and personal ornaments.

show.text: Bacho Kiro, the site twice | Lived in: about 45,000 years ago | Fossils reported: 2020

say.text: It was not a warm place. Animal bones from the cave show a subarctic climate about 45,000 years ago, much colder than once thought.

show.text: Subarctic cold, about 45,000 years ago

say.text: And Neanderthals were still around. The oldest people in the cave lived while Neanderthals were still living in Europe.

show.text: Homo sapiens in the cave | Neanderthals still in Europe | Cold, subarctic weather

say.text: Genetics adds a twist. A later person from the cave, about 35,000 years old, came from a genetically different group.

show.text: Early Europeans: groups replaced by later groups

say.text: Researchers say the earliest history of modern humans in Europe may have involved population replacements. The early cave group did not contribute to the genes of modern Europeans.

show.text: First arrivals did not all leave descendants | Later groups replaced earlier ones

ask.q: What does the genetic evidence suggest about the earliest Europeans?
ask.right: Some early groups were replaced by later ones
wrong: All modern Europeans descend from the first cave people
They never met Neanderthals
They all arrived by boat
ask.why: The 35,000-year-old person was from a different group, and the early cave group did not pass genes to modern Europeans.

say.text: Quick recap. Early exits, a main exit around 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, a sea crossing to Australia, and cold Europe about 45,000 years ago. Now the Americas.

show.text: Early exits | Main exit | Sea crossing to Australia | Europe about 45,000 years ago | Next: the Americas

say.text: In the ice age, so much water was locked in ice that sea level fell. A land bridge called Beringia joined Asia and North America.

show.text: Asia and North America joined by a wide land bridge, Beringia, with huge ice sheets to the south and east

say.text: For decades, the standard story was 'Clovis first'. Clovis hunters made stone tools about 13,000 years ago and were thought to be first, walking south through the ice-free corridor.

show.text: Clovis first + ice-free corridor

say.text: The ice-free corridor is a gap between two great ice sheets, the Cordilleran and the Laurentide. The big question is when it opened.

show.text: A narrow strip of land between two huge ice sheets running north to south

ask.right: A gap between two great ice sheets
wrong: A tunnel under the ice
A sea route along the coast
A bridge over the Atlantic
ask.why: As the ice sheets melted and retreated, the gap between them is what we call the corridor.

say.text: Dating suggests it began opening from the south about 15,400 years ago. The whole length was not open until after people were already arriving.

show.text: 15,400 years ago: it began to open

say.text: One study put the full opening at about 13,800 years ago, too late for the first peoples. So if people were in the Americas earlier, they must have come another way.

show.text: 13,800 years ago: fully open

ask.q: What did the new dating say about the corridor?
ask.right: It opened too late to be the road for the first Americans
wrong: It never existed
It opened before the ice age
It was open the whole time
ask.why: People had reached the Americas before the whole corridor opened, so it was not the first road.

say.text: The other idea is a coastal route. In 2007 Jon Erlandson and colleagues proposed a 'kelp highway': boat travel down the Pacific coast, following rich waters.

show.text: Kelp highway: a coastal route by boat

say.text: Some researchers add winter sea ice as a possible road. The evidence is thin: few coastal sites that old, but similar gaps exist along the corridor route.

show.text: Boats along the coast | Winter sea ice | Few coastal sites that old, so far

ask.right: A proposed coastal route by boat along the Pacific shore, following rich sea life
wrong: A road made of seaweed linking Asia and America
A path along an inland river
Another name for the ice-free corridor
ask.why: The kelp highway is the idea that people travelled the Pacific coast, where kelp forests supported food from the sea.

say.text: Now newer finds. Cooper's Ferry in western Idaho shows people about 16,000 years ago, over a thousand years before the corridor is thought to have opened.

show.text: Cooper's Ferry, the site twice | Lived in: about 16,000 years ago | Results published: 2019

say.text: It lies more than 500 kilometres inland, so those people may have followed rivers inland from a coastal route. Not everyone agrees the tools prove a coastal link.

show.text: A river running inland from the Pacific coast to Cooper's Ferry, Idaho

say.text: White Sands in New Mexico has human footprints pressed into mud beside an ancient lake. They were first found in 2009 and excavated in 2019.

show.text: Human footprints in pale clay at White Sands National Park

say.text: A 2021 paper dated them to between 21,000 and 23,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum. So the site twice: made then, found in 2009.

show.text: White Sands, the site twice | Footprints made: about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago | First found 2009, excavated 2019, published 2021

say.text: They were first dated using seeds of a water plant. Critics worried such plants can take in old carbon, which could make the dates too old.

show.text: Old carbon worry: water plants may make dates look too old

say.text: So in 2023 scientists dated pollen and used sediment luminescence and got the same age. In 2025 a team dated lake mud at 20,700 to 22,400 years.

show.text: Seeds: 21,000 to 23,000 | Pollen and luminescence (2023): same age | Lake mud (2025): 20,700 to 22,400

ask.q: Why did scientists redo the White Sands dating with other materials?
ask.right: To check whether the water-plant seeds had given dates that were too old
wrong: Because the footprints had washed away
To find out who made the footprints
Because radiocarbon cannot date seeds
ask.why: If different materials give the same age, the first date is much more likely to be right.

say.text: Still, not everyone is convinced. Archaeologist Waters says he remains concerned about the radiocarbon ages, even with the new data.

show.text: Accepted by many, not by everyone

say.text: One more site: Monte Verde in southern Chile, found in late 1975 about 800 kilometres south of Santiago. A peat bog kept wood, leather, rope and the remains of wooden huts.

show.text: A creek bank in southern Chile where preserved wood and hut remains were dug from peat

say.text: Tom Dillehay's team dated the people there to about 14,500 years ago. That helped break 'Clovis first', after a long and exhausting fight.

show.text: Monte Verde, the site twice | Lived in: about 14,500 years ago (disputed) | Found: late 1975

say.text: A recent study in Science says the site may be much younger, perhaps only about 8,000 years old. Dillehay's team replied that the evidence still supports 14,500 years.

show.text: Monte Verde: 14,500 years old, or much younger? | Challenge: perhaps 8,000 years | Reply: still about 14,500

say.text: Some experts called the new study poor geological work. So this argument is live and unsettled.

show.text: Live argument

ask.q: What is being argued about Monte Verde?
ask.right: Whether people lived there about 14,500 years ago or much more recently
wrong: Whether the site is in Chile
Whether Clovis points were found there
Whether the peat bog still exists
ask.why: The site's age is the dispute. If it is younger, it no longer shows people in South America so early.

say.text: Here are the main dates for the Americas. Remember that every bar is a claim that someone has tested, and some are still argued.

show.text: Dates in the debate over the first Americans

say.text: Why are these dates argued over? Small groups leave few traces. Sand can be disturbed. Water plants can carry old carbon. And each new find can move the date.

show.text: Few traces from small groups | Disturbed sand | Old carbon in water plants | New finds change dates

ask.q: Which is a real reason dates are argued over?
ask.right: Disturbed sediment or old carbon can make a date look too old
wrong: Archaeologists refuse to use science
All sites agree already
Dates are never checked again
ask.why: We saw this at Madjedbebe (disturbed sand) and White Sands (old carbon). Scientists keep rechecking.

say.text: Next class we turn from the road to the mind: art, symbols and cave paintings.

show.text: Next: art, symbols and the mind

notes.topic: Madjedbebe rock shelter: people there about 65,000 years ago (disputed); dug in the 1970s, 1989 and for the 2017 study
Apidima Cave: skulls about 210,000 years old; found late 1970s, reanalysed 2019
Bacho Kiro Cave: Homo sapiens about 45,000 years ago; fossils reported 2020
Cooper's Ferry: people there about 16,000 years ago; results published 2019
White Sands footprints: made about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago; first found 2009, excavated 2019
Monte Verde: people there about 14,500 years ago (disputed); found late 1975

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: A Homo sapiens skull and, tens of thousands of years later, a Neanderthal skull were left in the same cave in Greece.
Neanderthals were still living in Europe, in the cold subarctic climate that the first Homo sapiens at Bacho Kiro Cave also faced.
The Last Glacial Maximum: ice sheets were at their fullest, and the White Sands area was a wetland with ice age animals.
The last ice age was starting to fade, and Monte Verde sat in a cool, wet temperate rain forest about 60 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean.

other_side.claim: People reached Australia about 65,000 years ago, based on Madjedbebe.
other_side.other_view: Archaeologists Jim Allen and James O'Connell argue the sand at Madjedbebe was disturbed and that younger artefacts could have moved into older sand. They say the other oldest Sahul sites cluster between about 43,000 and 54,000 years ago, so the date of arrival is about 50,000 years ago. The excavation team reports only small-scale disturbance and no extensive termite reworking.

other_side.claim: Early crossings to Sahul show planned open-sea voyages.
other_side.other_view: The 2019 model concludes that people could plan voyages lasting several days by at least 50,000 years ago. The authors state that whether these particular crossings were accidental or intentional is unknown.

other_side.claim: The 210,000-year-old Apidima 1 skull is an early Homo sapiens.
other_side.other_view: The 2019 Nature study concluded this, but some summaries say the skull fragment cannot be confidently assigned to Homo sapiens. The identification is still open.

other_side.claim: The ice-free corridor opened too late to be the first route into the Americas.
other_side.other_view: One study dates the full opening of the corridor to about 13,800 years ago. Others argue that evidence for coastal sites that old is also thin, and say Clovis-like peoples probably did move through the corridor later as it opened.

other_side.claim: Cooper's Ferry, dated to about 16,000 years ago, supports an early coastal route.
other_side.other_view: Archaeologist David Meltzer is not convinced that the stemmed-point tools clearly predate Clovis or show a link around the Pacific Rim, and notes that the complete points are almost the same age as Clovis.

other_side.claim: The White Sands footprints are 21,000 to 23,000 years old.
other_side.other_view: Seeds, pollen, luminescence and lake mud all gave matching ages. Archaeologist Waters says he is still concerned about the radiocarbon ages.

other_side.claim: Monte Verde II is about 14,500 years old.
other_side.other_view: A recent Science study says the site may be only about 8,000 years old, and some experts criticise its geology. Dillehay's team replied that geological and archaeological evidence supports 14,500 years.
